title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
authors: Valeria Repetto, Romina D'Aurizio, Piero Farinelli
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.

infographic.key_insight: Soft-MoQE learns input-dependent combinations of fixed quantum feature maps, avoiding quantum-parameter optimization while achieving task-dependent performance comparable to a trainable quantum neural network.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Moving trainable routing to a classical network reduces quantum training cost by orders of magnitude in the reported benchmarks.
method: Build a heterogeneous pool of fixed, non-trainable quantum circuits.
Train a classical gating network to weight each circuit's embedding per input.
Combine quantum embeddings using the learned soft routing.
infographic.evidence_signal: On PCA-reduced MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST tasks, Soft-MoQE outperforms the best single expert, uniform expert averaging, and a linear baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation is limited to three PCA-reduced image tasks; scalability and robustness on noisy quantum hardware remain unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning

title: Variational Relevance-Informed Sparsification of Term Measurements for Variational Quantum Algorithms
authors: Yifeng Peng, Bin Yan, Harshal Shah, Srinivasan Raghuraman, Kim Wagner, Sunpreet Singh Arora
abstract: Repeated measurements are a major bottleneck in variational quantum algorithms (VQAs). We uncover and characterize parameter-specific sparsity in the matrix of qubit-wise commuting (QWC) group contributions to parameter-shift gradients: most absolute contribution mass concentrates in a subset of groups whose relevance varies across parameters and optimization states. Building on this structure, we introduce a learned controller that predicts group relevance from Hamiltonian, circuit, light-cone, and current-state features, then selects measurements through a tunable coverage threshold. Exact contributions provide offline supervision without being required at deployment. Across 15 molecular VQE settings, our method saves 49.6% of nominal gradient-measurement shots with a mean absolute energy gap of 5.67 mHa to Full-QWC. We then ask whether large language models (LLMs) can solve the same selection problem without fine-tuning. The results reveal both promise and a clear limitation: LLMs can identify useful measurement groups, yet without guidance, local models do not consistently prioritize the physical information that matters most. Our learned controller uses these cues more effectively. This contrast points toward a broader direction for AI-assisted science: combining the flexibility of general-purpose models with explicit physical representations, task-specific objectives, and domain-grounded validation.

infographic.key_insight: Parameter-specific sparsity lets a learned controller focus quantum gradient measurements on the qubit-wise commuting groups that matter most.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Relevance-guided measurement selection can reduce variational quantum algorithm shot costs while retaining energy accuracy close to full-group measurement.
method: Characterize sparse group contributions to parameter-shift gradients.
Predict group relevance from Hamiltonian, circuit, light-cone, and current-state features.
Select groups using a tunable coverage threshold, with exact contributions needed only for offline supervision.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 15 molecular VQE settings, the method saved 49.6% of nominal gradient-measurement shots with a mean absolute energy gap of 5.67 mHa relative to Full-QWC.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the evaluated molecular settings remains unestablished, and nominal shot savings do not alone establish end-to-end runtime gains.
infographic.paper_title: Variational Relevance-Informed Sparsification of Term Measurements for Variational Quantum Algorithms

title: Nonlinear function regression using quantum ensemble learning
authors: Yueen Chen, Mohammad Sharifian, Abolfazl Bayat
abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and quantum technologies have driven the emergence of quantum machine learning, yet imperfections in near-term quantum devices remain a major obstacle for achieving practical quantum advantage. In the absence of fault-tolerant machines, ensemble learning, which combines multiple imperfect quantum devices, may unlock new quantum computing applications. Here, we introduce two ensemble-learning algorithms, namely Bagging and AdaBoost, for enhancing the accuracy of nonlinear regression problems. While Bagging trains variational quantum regressors independently, AdaBoost employs a sequential training strategy and achieves significantly better prediction accuracy. By incorporating systematic feature selection into our ensemble learning algorithms, we enhance their predictive power for highly nonlinear functions. We further improve prediction accuracy through a feature-to-qubit mapping strategy based on repeated feature encoding. The performance of our ensemble-based algorithms improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using four benchmarking functions with varying degrees of nonlinearity by relying on a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.

infographic.key_insight: Ensembles of variational quantum regressors improve nonlinear regression accuracy, with sequential AdaBoost outperforming independently trained Bagging.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining imperfect quantum regressors offers a potential route to more accurate prediction on near-term quantum hardware without requiring fault tolerance.
method: Train quantum regressors independently with Bagging or sequentially with AdaBoost.
Select features systematically from first- and second-order polynomial terms.
Use repeated feature encoding in the feature-to-qubit mapping to improve accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on four benchmark functions of varying nonlinearity shows accuracy improving with both ensemble size and individual regressor size.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish practical quantum advantage or quantify hardware-noise robustness and ensemble training costs.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlinear function regression using quantum ensemble learning

title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
authors: Eduardo Reck Miranda, Moein Fahmideh Vatandoost
abstract: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum reinforcement learning enables musical agents to develop distinct compositional behaviours through reward-driven interaction rather than large-corpus imitation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A hybrid quantum–classical framework connects parameterised quantum circuits with MIDI-based workflows for adaptive computer-aided composition and performance.
method: Represent musical agents as parameterised quantum circuits updated through reinforcement learning.
Use atomistic agents for separate pitch and rhythm decisions, or holistic agents for unified pitch–duration events.
Combine and weight musically grounded rewards to shape distinct agent mindsets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports generalisation to unseen musical material, interactive and offline MIDI demonstrations, and musically meaningful learning on IBM quantum hardware, without quantitative metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish a quantum advantage over classical reinforcement learning or quantify scalability on current hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning

title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
authors: Zhi-Lei Zhang, Lianxiang Cui, C. P. Sun, Kohei Nakajima, Kazuyuki Aihara
abstract: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

infographic.key_insight: Topological quantum reservoir computing combines long-lived Majorana edge modes for memory with fast bulk dynamics for information processing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could harness protected quantum degrees of freedom for temporal learning without requiring universal logical-qubit computation.
method: Use a one-dimensional Kitaev chain as a quantum reservoir.
Match input interfaces to enable programmable writing into protected memory.
Use interactions to autonomously consolidate information from bulk dynamics into edge modes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved performance on tasks requiring long-term temporal retention in a Kitaev-chain study, but provides no quantitative metrics or hardware results.
infographic.watch_item: Accessing protected memory introduces tradeoffs, making interface design and reliable bulk-to-edge transfer key implementation concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing

title: Quantum Annealing with a Quantum Neural Network: Width of Annealing Matters
authors: Mojtaba Asadollahi, Danial Khajehzadeh, Abolfazl Ramezanpour
abstract: Quantum annealing is a promising quantum algorithm for dealing with computationally hard optimization problems. Currently available hardware can implement the algorithm for a significant class of Hamiltonian problems. However, its performance is especially limited in discontinuous quantum phase transitions, where the energy gap shrinks exponentially with system size. In this paper, we introduce an extension of quantum annealing to a quantum neural network and study its performance in a number of prototypical optimization problems. In particular, we observe that already a random quantum annealing network of width W = 2 can exponentially reduce the number of evolution layers or depth of the annealing process in the quantum search problem. By tuning the network parameters the search problem can be solved with exponentially small errors by a quantum perceptron of depth L = 1 and width W = 2. The findings show that width of a quantum annealing network is critical to enhance the success probability of the algorithm by providing a larger and learnable evolution space for the annealing process.

infographic.key_insight: Widening a quantum annealing network to W = 2 can exponentially reduce the required evolution depth for quantum search.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Network width and trainable parameters offer design levers for improving quantum optimization beyond simply extending annealing depth.
method: Extend quantum annealing to a quantum neural network.
Evaluate performance on prototypical optimization problems.
Compare random networks with parameter-tuned quantum perceptrons.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports exponential depth reduction for random W = 2 networks in quantum search and exponentially small errors for a tuned perceptron with L = 1 and W = 2.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish hardware feasibility, parameter-training cost, or whether the quantum-search gains generalize to other optimization problems.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Annealing with a Quantum Neural Network: Width of Annealing Matters

title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits
authors: Davi Castro-Silva, Ryan Dancy, Sergii Strelchuk
abstract: Symmetric circuits require every symmetry of the input to extend to an automorphism of the circuit. In the classical setting, their connection to descriptive complexity yields strong unconditional lower bounds. We extend this approach to the quantum model of symmetric computation defined by Castro-Silva, Gur, and Strelchuk (ITCS 2026), proving a tradeoff between circuit size and entanglement width (the smallest $b$ such that, on every computational-basis input, the state after each layer factors into states on at most $b$ qubits each). Our main result identifies a graph property decidable in classical polynomial time that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits on $n$-vertex graphs with entanglement width $o(n/\log n)$ can compute. The bound holds for circuits with arbitrary one-qubit and two-qubit gates and unrestricted depth, and remains valid under the weaker notion of symmetry with respect to even permutations of vertices. Our proof is based on a new quantum pebble game based on the partial trace. The resulting indistinguishability theorem transfers classical pebble-game lower bounds to quantum circuits with restricted entanglement. By contrast, without entanglement restrictions, we show that every graph property in BQP can be computed by a uniform family of polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits. Restricting to circuits with no entanglement at all, we show that polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width 1 can compute every graph property definable in fixed-point logic with counting. Finally, we give an efficient symmetric implementation of QAOA for MAX 3XOR, providing a starting point for studying entanglement lower bounds in quantum optimization algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: Some classically polynomial-time graph properties cannot be computed by polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits whose entanglement width is o(n/log n), even with unrestricted depth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For symmetry-preserving quantum circuit design, entanglement width is a provable resource bottleneck that additional depth alone cannot overcome.
method: Define entanglement width through the largest factor block needed after each layer on computational-basis inputs.
Introduce a partial-trace quantum pebble game to transfer classical indistinguishability lower bounds.
Construct symmetric circuits for BQP graph properties without entanglement restrictions and an efficient symmetric QAOA implementation for MAX 3XOR.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical proofs and circuit constructions, not experimental benchmarks; the lower bound covers arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates and even-permutation symmetry.
infographic.watch_item: The lower bound applies to symmetric circuit families, not unrestricted quantum circuits, and does not establish a practical QAOA advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits

title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
authors: Aleksandra Świerkowska, Ilgaz Er, Emmanouil Giortamis, Pramod Bhatotia
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires continuous quantum error correction (QEC) to suppress physical noise. While Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, universal computation breaks this paradigm: executing non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard, real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements. Consequently, the controller must extract syndromes, decode them, and update the Pauli frame in real time, closing the entire QEC loop within a strict $1\,μ\text{s}$ cycle. However, prior proposals on Pauli frame tracking remain largely theoretical, leaving the microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed control pipelines unaddressed. To this end, we present QuFrame, a control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking that closes the QEC loop within $1\,μ\text{s}$ while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. By introducing QuFrameISA, we cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. To strictly guarantee the $1\,μ\text{s}$ deadline, QuFrame pairs an asynchronous primary decoder with an on-chip fallback decoder that resolves in $144\,\text{ns}$, natively reconciling divergent updates in hardware without degrading logical error rates.

infographic.key_insight: QuFrame enables real-time Pauli frame tracking for fault-tolerant quantum control, closing the QEC loop within a 1 μs cycle while sustaining QPU-rate throughput.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It addresses time-critical dependencies between error-corrected measurements and non-Clifford gate execution, where software-only deferred corrections are insufficient.
method: QuFrameISA separates instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management.
Per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines use a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit supports independent, lock-free concurrent commits.
An asynchronous primary decoder is paired with an on-chip fallback decoder and hardware reconciliation of divergent updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 144 ns fallback decoding and a 1 μs QEC-loop deadline without degraded logical error rates, but provides no evaluation setup or benchmark details.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability and timing guarantees require validation under realistic decoder workloads, communication delays, and hardware resource constraints.
infographic.paper_title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control

title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control
authors: Christopher A. Pattison, Jeongwan Haah, John Preskill
abstract: Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with $n$ physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/ε)$ logical qubits, where $ε$ is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/ε)$; an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to ${\sf polylog}(n/ε)$.

infographic.key_insight: A fault-tolerant quantum processor can support universal computation using a constant number of external control wires and a fixed, periodically repeated local circuit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture offers a route to reducing quantum-chip control wiring and off-chip syndrome traffic, trading control simplicity for execution overhead.
method: Propel quantum information through a planar array using a fixed, clocked, geometrically local depth-3 circuit.
Stream classical instructions through a constant number of external wires, each connected to one qubit.
Prove an accuracy threshold under noisy gates, measurements, and wires, assuming a noiseless global clock.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical threshold theorem, not hardware measurements: n physical qubits support n/polylog(n/ε) logical qubits with error ε per logical gate.
infographic.watch_item: The baseline takes n/polylog(n/ε) time per logical gate; faster polylogarithmic timing requires idealized instantaneous, noiseless on-chip classical broadcasts.
infographic.paper_title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control

title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
authors: Luca Hofele, Yongxin Song, Áron Márton, Ian Hesner, Ilya Besedin, Jakob Ekert
abstract: Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

infographic.key_insight: Lattice surgery enabled logical-state teleportation between two distance-three surface-code qubits on a 41-physical-qubit superconducting circuit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Repeated stabilizer measurements and shorter, lower-gate-count protocols improved teleportation fidelity, informing practical logical-operation design.
method: Merge two surface-code patches using lattice surgery.
Track logical observables as information transfers from source to target.
Repeat stabilizer measurements and optimize gate count and sequence duration.
infographic.evidence_signal: The experiment observed increased teleported-state fidelity with repeated post-merge stabilizer measurements and further gains from protocol optimization; the abstract provides no numerical fidelities.
infographic.watch_item: Results at code distance three do not establish performance or resource requirements at larger, fault-tolerant computational scales.
infographic.paper_title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits

title: Gutzwiller Quantum-Classical Embedding for Dynamics Simulations of Correlated Electron Systems
authors: Joshua Aftergood, Daniele Guerci, Jacob Brunton, Feng Zhang, Thomas Iadecola, Peter P. Orth
abstract: Simulating the real-time dynamics of correlated electron systems requires a nonperturbative treatment of local correlations over long times, a challenge for classical methods. We present the time-dependent Gutzwiller quantum-classical embedding framework, t-GQCE, for generic multi-orbital lattice models with time-dependent Hamiltonians. Within the time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation, the lattice dynamics is mapped onto a noninteracting quasiparticle lattice, propagated classically, coupled to finite interacting embedding models propagated on quantum processors. The two parts exchange only embedding Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices, and the framework is agnostic to the quantum dynamics solver. We demonstrate it with adaptive variational quantum dynamics simulations of interaction quenches in the Hubbard model on the Bethe lattice. Without ghost orbitals, the embedding problem reduces to a single qubit, simulated on IBM quantum hardware with two qubits, including an ancilla. With more ghost orbitals, t-GQCE suppresses the artificial undamped oscillations of the conventional Gutzwiller approximation and approaches nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory results for weak and strong quenches. Statevector simulations with 2, 4 and 6 ghost orbitals per spin, or 8, 12 and 16 qubits, give adaptive circuits that follow the embedding states with infidelities below $5\times10^{-4}$. Under trapped-ion noise models, circuit compression, measurements in rotated orbital bases with post-selection, and noise mitigation reduce the measurement errors severalfold. At one third of the error rates of a hardware-benchmarked noise model, they reach an accuracy of $0.01$ for the single-particle density matrix and the double occupancy with $10^5$ shots per time step, and the Quantinuum H2-Emulator gives similar accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: t-GQCE combines classical lattice propagation with quantum embedding dynamics to capture correlated-electron evolution, approaching nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory results as ghost orbitals are added.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework assigns finite interacting problems to quantum processors while keeping noninteracting lattice dynamics classical, exchanging only Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices.
method: Map lattice dynamics to coupled quasiparticle and interacting embedding models using the time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation.
Propagate the lattice classically and embedding states with a quantum dynamics solver.
Use adaptive circuits, circuit compression, rotated-basis measurements, post-selection, and noise mitigation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Hubbard-model quench tests achieved embedding-state infidelities below 5×10⁻⁴ in 8–16-qubit statevector simulations; reduced-noise tests reached 0.01 accuracy for density matrices and double occupancy with 10⁵ shots per time step.
infographic.watch_item: The reported noisy-simulation accuracy required mitigation and error rates one third of a hardware-benchmarked model; the IBM hardware demonstration used only one embedding qubit plus an ancilla.
infographic.paper_title: Gutzwiller Quantum-Classical Embedding for Dynamics Simulations of Correlated Electron Systems

title: General Noise Channels and Mid-Circuit Measurements for Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batched Execution
authors: Louis Follet, Paavai Pari, Isidor Schoch, Thien Nguyen, Justin G. Lietz, Daniel Lowell
abstract: Many studies of quantum protocols require fast sampling of large amounts of measurement data from noisy quantum circuits, such as for training machine-learning decoders for quantum error correction. Exact simulation of realistic noise is expensive, while stabilizer-based simulators are fast but approximate, for example through Pauli twirling, which generally alters the output statistics. Pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) accelerates exact trajectory simulation by sampling noise before state evolution. This method requires the outcome probability of every stochastic event to be independent of the state, which excludes mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels. We present a generalization of PTSBE to measurement and Kraus operators without approximation. Each event is partially pre-sampled, while deferred outcomes are drawn during grouped execution via multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. We implement the method for GPUs as an extension of CUDA-Q. On distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, it is up to 24x faster than conventional trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q. On 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, it is up to 83x faster and outperforms the near-Clifford simulator Clifft when more than about 25% of the gates are non-Clifford. With repeated sampling of each final state, its sampling rate per trajectory exceeds that of CUDA-Q by nearly five orders of magnitude. Our method also allows us to compare exact amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled channel on a surface-code memory, revealing that twirling overestimates the detection rate by 21% and raises the logical error rate of a lookup decoder by 8%. This work makes exact, high-throughput simulation practical for general noisy circuits, from data generation for training decoders to studying measurement-based fault-tolerant protocols under realistic noise.

infographic.key_insight: Generalized pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution enables exact, high-throughput simulation of noisy quantum circuits with general Kraus channels and mid-circuit measurements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The GPU-based CUDA-Q extension accelerates realistic quantum-error-correction data generation without relying on noise approximations such as Pauli twirling.
method: Partially pre-sample stochastic events before state evolution.
Resolve deferred outcomes during grouped execution using multinomial branching.
Reuse cached states to reduce repeated simulation work.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported speedups over conventional CUDA-Q trajectory sampling reach 24× for distance-3 topological code memories and 83× for 30-qubit random circuits; Pauli twirling overestimated detection rates by 21% and increased lookup-decoder logical error rates by 8% in a surface-code memory comparison.
infographic.watch_item: Reported speedups are workload-specific; performance and GPU memory requirements should be validated for larger circuits and different branching patterns.
infographic.paper_title: General Noise Channels and Mid-Circuit Measurements for Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batched Execution

title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
authors: Hansol Noh, Unam Oh, Sangkyu Baek, Doyeol, Ahn
abstract: Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.

infographic.key_insight: Reduced-order models paired with quantum transport can preserve nonlinear flow dynamics while making per-step rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with grid resolution at fixed model dimension and polynomial degree.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach makes reduced-model polynomial degree a practical trade-off between flow-model accuracy and early fault-tolerant quantum resource costs.
method: Fit polynomial reduced-order flow models using sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics.
Encode probability-density evolution with Walsh-synthesized Koopman–von Neumann transport.
Estimate end-to-end runtime and physical-qubit requirements using surface-code resource models.
infographic.evidence_signal: For a saturating cylinder wake, the study estimates 1.62 hours on about 560,000 physical qubits for 1% relative RMS field error against the radial model, and demonstrates nonlinear radial transport on IBM hardware with reference-circuit noise mitigation.
infographic.watch_item: These are fault-tolerant resource estimates rather than demonstrated end-to-end runtimes; three-coordinate wake estimates range from hours to weeks, and the stated 1% error is measured against a reduced radial model.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime

title: Residual-Algebraic Design of Symmetry-Preserving Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Sahinur Reja
abstract: Symmetry-preserving (SP) variational quantum circuits restrict evolution to physically relevant sectors of Hilbert space, but symmetry preservation alone does not guarantee accessibility within those sectors. We show that a restricted generator set can possess a residual dynamical Lie algebra whose commutant further decomposes the target symmetry sector into invariant blocks. The associated block populations are conserved and impose a kinematic upper bound on the fidelity with a target state. We then invert this diagnostic into a circuit-design principle: candidate SP generators can be screened before variational optimization by asking whether they break the residual commutant, which invariant blocks they couple, and what adjoint module they generate under the residual algebra. For two orthogonal residual blocks we prove that a single elementary real inter-block rotation generates the full orthogonal algebra. We further derive a complex escape criterion: if the real and imaginary parts of an inter-block seed are independent over the residual intertwiner algebra, the generated module is the full complex coupling space and the enlarged algebra becomes special unitary. A connected residual-block graph yields a natural multi-block generalization and suggests minimum-cost spanning-tree circuit design. We demonstrate this design principle in the XXZ and Hubbard models, where residual-algebra screening identifies SP circuit extensions that remove the relevant accessibility obstructions. These examples establish a unified route from residual-symmetry diagnosis and fidelity bounds to predictive quantum circuit design.

infographic.key_insight: Symmetry-preserving quantum circuits can still be trapped in invariant subspaces, but residual Lie-algebra analysis identifies added generators that restore accessibility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Screening generators before optimization can guide symmetry-preserving circuit design and avoid ansätze with structural fidelity limits.
method: Identify residual commutants, invariant blocks, and conserved populations to bound target-state fidelity.
Screen added generators by the blocks they couple and the adjoint modules they generate.
Use real and complex coupling criteria to enlarge the dynamical algebra, with connected block graphs guiding multi-block designs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports algebraic proofs and demonstrations in XXZ and Hubbard models, but provides no quantitative performance benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Removing algebraic accessibility obstructions does not by itself guarantee shallow circuits, noise robustness, or efficient variational optimization.
infographic.paper_title: Residual-Algebraic Design of Symmetry-Preserving Variational Quantum Circuits

title: Efficient simulation of variational quantum circuits: representation, accuracy and CPU/GPU allocation
authors: Vojtěch Novák, Radovan Rečka, Ondřej Knebl, Ivan Zelinka
abstract: Classical circuit simulation supports quantum software development and verification and provides a baseline for assessing quantum advantage. We compare gate-based statevector simulation, direct Pauli evolution and matrix product states for molecular and spin Variational Hamiltonian Ansatze and hardware-efficient ansatze on CPU/GPU systems, varying width, depth, precision and resource allocation. In the tested implementations, direct Pauli evolution benefits complex molecular VHA, whereas GPUs accelerate wider spin and hardware efficient circuits. Matrix product state is useful when limited entanglement permits accurate compression; corrected CPU FP32 can meet the tested tolerance while costing more than FP64. Workload size, startup, worker memory and task-specific profiling can change the preferred allocation. Matched NumPy Pauli updates accelerate two-layer full LiH by 3.45-fold; the GPU gives approximately 30-fold acceleration over 18-thread Aer for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM, both in FP64. We provide a procedure for choosing representation, precision and worker allocation jointly, comparing the cost of complete energy evaluations under accuracy, memory and core constraints.

infographic.key_insight: Efficient variational quantum circuit simulation requires jointly choosing representation, precision and CPU/GPU allocation for each workload.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Benchmark complete energy evaluations under accuracy, memory and core constraints rather than assuming one simulator or device is always fastest.
method: Compare gate-based statevectors, direct Pauli evolution and matrix product states.
Test molecular and spin variational Hamiltonian ansatze and hardware-efficient circuits across width, depth and precision.
Profile CPU/GPU and worker allocations while checking accuracy and memory use.
infographic.evidence_signal: In FP64 tests, matched NumPy Pauli updates accelerated two-layer full LiH by 3.45×, while a GPU delivered approximately 30× acceleration over 18-thread Aer for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on implementation and workload: startup overhead, worker memory and entanglement-limited compression can change the preferred configuration.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient simulation of variational quantum circuits: representation, accuracy and CPU/GPU allocation

title: Environment-assisted imaginary time evolution in feedback-based quantum algorithms
authors: J. C. Bellizotti Souza, M. C. de Oliveira
abstract: The Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) prepares ground states without classical parameter optimization, but requires deep circuits and can stagnate away from the ground state as a consequence of barren plateaus and symmetry protection. In order to avoid stagnation, imaginary time evolution (ITE) layers can be incorporated into FALQON layers, enhancing FALQON convergence. However, applying a non-unitary ITE layer in a closed quantum system is not possible, and approximations must be made to use ITE on real hardware; using an open quantum system formulation to incorporate ITE into FALQON represents a better approach. We describe ITE as a quantum operation induced by an environment, and combine it with the FALQON feedback law. In simulations of a frustrated Ising chain (ANNNI) and of MaxCut, the resulting algorithm prepares the ground state starting from any initial state, where FALQON can fail, and needs fewer layers on average when the initial state is fixed for the two investigated problems. The CITE-FALQON advantage strongly depends on the system phase for the ANNNI chain, and on the graph weights for the MaxCut problem.

infographic.key_insight: Environment-assisted imaginary time evolution helps FALQON escape stagnation and reach ground states in simulated quantum optimization problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining environmental quantum operations with feedback control could reduce circuit-layer requirements without classical parameter optimization.
method: Represent imaginary time evolution as a quantum operation induced by an environment.
Combine this operation with the FALQON feedback law in CITE-FALQON.
Simulate ground-state preparation for a frustrated ANNNI Ising chain and MaxCut.
infographic.evidence_signal: For the two simulated problems, CITE-FALQON reached ground states from any initial state and used fewer layers on average in fixed-initial-state comparisons, including cases where FALQON failed.
infographic.watch_item: Hardware feasibility remains to be established, and the advantage depends strongly on the ANNNI phase and MaxCut graph weights.
infographic.paper_title: Environment-assisted imaginary time evolution in feedback-based quantum algorithms

title: QCCDCert: Formally Verified Compilation for QCCD Co-Design
authors: John Zhuoyang Ye, Jens Palsberg, Ke Sun, Hartmut Haeffner
abstract: Quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architectures enable scalable trapped-ion quantum computing by dynamically shuttling ions between specialized processing and storage zones. A QCCD can be built with many trap sizes and layouts. Comparing them requires compiling every program under each design's transport, capacity and control constraints, and trusting the target code of each compilation. We present a co-design framework built on one Lean-verified compiler. The hardware description and its operating rules are compiler inputs, so a single theorem covers every candidate design: the target code of every compilation preserves its program's behavior and obeys the hardware rules. Across 75 benchmark programs of 11 to 130 qubits, the best design found takes 66% less modeled execution time on average than the worst design of equal capacity. An AI agent that proposes devices based on our compiler's checked results beats the fastest of these designs on 71 of 75 programs. Our verified compiler provably avoids the 11 defects that we report in three previous compilers. It scales to hundreds of qubits, compiling 512-qubit programs for a 38-trap device in 1 to 29 minutes.

infographic.key_insight: QCCDCert uses one Lean-verified compiler to explore QCCD hardware designs while proving that compiled programs preserve behavior and obey each design’s hardware rules.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can compare trapped-ion layouts, trap sizes, and operating constraints with formally verified compilation rather than trusting separate compiler implementations.
method: Supply hardware descriptions and operating rules as compiler inputs.
Use a single correctness theorem covering all supported candidate designs.
Guide an AI agent’s device proposals with compiler-checked results.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 75 benchmarks with 11–130 qubits, the best evaluated design averaged 66% less modeled execution time than the worst equal-capacity design; AI-proposed devices beat the fastest evaluated design on 71 benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Reported speedups are based on modeled execution time, so physical-device gains depend on how faithfully the hardware rules and timing models capture real operation.
infographic.paper_title: QCCDCert: Formally Verified Compilation for QCCD Co-Design

title: Perturbative Recovery of Stabilizer-Subspace Correlations for Quantum Computational Chemistry
authors: Qianjun Yao, Jie Liu, He Li
abstract: Stabilizer-based subspace methods can substantially reduce the quantum resources required for electronic structure calculations, but the resulting projection neglects Hamiltonian couplings to configurations outside the retained subspace. In this work, we introduce Stabilizer-Subspace Perturbation Theory (SSPT) to recover the associated correlation contributions, using the Contextual Subspace Variational Quantum Eigensolver (CS-VQE) as a representative application. The central idea is to exploit the Pauli terms eliminated by stabilizer projection as perturbative operators that generate an external manifold from the optimized reference state. Their energetic contributions are evaluated using an Epstein-Nesbet-type second-order correction or a resolvent-based formulation that retains couplings within the external space. By exploiting the factorized structure of the stabilizer-constrained reference state, the required matrix elements can be evaluated through Pauli expectation values on the reduced contextual register without explicitly reconstructing the full-space wave function. Molecular benchmarks demonstrate substantial reductions in projection-induced energy errors, allowing chemical precision to be achieved with fewer contextual qubits in several cases. These results establish stabilizer-guided perturbation theory as a promising strategy for improving the accuracy of resource-efficient quantum chemistry calculations.

infographic.key_insight: Stabilizer-Subspace Perturbation Theory (SSPT) recovers correlation lost during stabilizer projection, improving quantum chemistry accuracy while retaining a reduced quantum register.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SSPT can reduce the contextual qubits needed for chemically precise energy estimates, making resource-efficient quantum chemistry calculations more practical.
method: Use Pauli terms eliminated by stabilizer projection to generate external states from an optimized reference.
Estimate correlation corrections with Epstein–Nesbet-type second-order perturbation theory or a resolvent retaining external-space couplings.
Evaluate matrix elements through reduced-register Pauli expectation values without reconstructing the full-space wave function.
infographic.evidence_signal: Molecular benchmarks show substantially reduced projection-induced energy errors and chemical precision with fewer contextual qubits in several cases, though the abstract provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: The measurement and classical processing costs of treating the external manifold require assessment as molecular systems grow.
infographic.paper_title: Perturbative Recovery of Stabilizer-Subspace Correlations for Quantum Computational Chemistry

title: Quantum Information Transfer in Molecular Polaritonic Networks: A Van Vleck Effective-Hamiltonian Approach
authors: Saad Yalouz, Vincent Pouthier
abstract: Achieving high-fidelity transfer of an arbitrary quantum state between spatially separated qubits is a central challenge for reliable quantum hardware. We address this question within a polaritonic framework by introducing Projected-Block Van Vleck Perturbation Theory (PB-VVPT). Based on quasidegenerate perturbation theory, this approach describes a molecular network coupled to an optical cavity and local phonons through a generalized Holstein--Tavis--Cummings Hamiltonian. Quantum information is encoded in a coherent superposition of exciton-cavity states, while phonons constitute a weakly coupled environment. In the nonadiabatic regime of weak exciton-phonon coupling, the method incorporates phonon-induced renormalization of polaritonic states and their dynamics while reducing the Hamiltonian to independent fixed-phonon-number sectors and coupled polaron-polariton subblocks. This structure provides efficient access to the coherence and population propagators governing quantum-state transfer without invoking a Markovian approximation. We benchmark the approach against exact dynamics for a molecular wheel network, considering both molecule-to-molecule and molecule-to-cavity transfer. PB-VVPT accurately reproduces short- and long-time transfer dynamics, including thermal decoherence and fidelity revivals consistent with non-Markovian memory effects, with prediction errors below $1\%$ over most of the simulated time intervals. This accuracy is achieved with an estimated diagonalization cost more than two orders of magnitude lower than that of the exact reference calculations. These results establish PB-VVPT as an accurate and computationally efficient approach to quantum information transfer in molecular polaritonic networks.

infographic.key_insight: Projected-Block Van Vleck Perturbation Theory (PB-VVPT) efficiently predicts quantum-state transfer in molecular polaritonic networks while capturing phonon-induced decoherence and fidelity revivals.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method could accelerate simulation and design of cavity-coupled molecular quantum-state-transfer architectures without assuming memoryless environmental dynamics.
method: Model molecular excitons, an optical cavity, and local phonons with a generalized Holstein–Tavis–Cummings Hamiltonian.
Use PB-VVPT to reduce the Hamiltonian into fixed-phonon-number sectors and coupled polaron–polariton subblocks.
Compute coherence and population propagators, including phonon-induced renormalization, without a Markovian approximation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against exact molecular-wheel simulations, PB-VVPT reproduced molecule-to-molecule and molecule-to-cavity transfer with errors below 1% over most simulated intervals and an estimated diagonalization cost more than 100 times lower.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is computational and assumes weak exciton–phonon coupling in the nonadiabatic regime; accuracy outside that regime remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Information Transfer in Molecular Polaritonic Networks: A Van Vleck Effective-Hamiltonian Approach

title: Depth-Dependent Collapse and Warm-Start Limits of a Symmetry-Preserving VQE for the J$_1$--J$_2$ Heisenberg Ring
authors: Soumyadip Sahoo, Sahinur Reja
abstract: Increasing circuit depth is expected to improve a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). We show that this expectation can fail, and that curing the failure does not guarantee the exact ground state. We study a symmetry-preserving ansatz of SingleExcitationMinus gates, started from the Néel state, on the frustrated spin-$1/2$ $J_1$--$J_2$ Heisenberg ring with $N=10$ and $12$ sites. With random initialization the fidelity, energy error, half-chain entropy and total spin change abruptly at intermediate depth ($L\approx 9$ for $N=10$, $L=10$--$12$ for $N=12$), giving improvement, degradation and recovery, a double-descent-like shape. The circuit family is nested and the gradient stays finite, so this is an optimization failure, not a loss of expressibility or a barren plateau. A chained warm start, which extends an optimized shallow circuit with identity layers, removes the collapse and improves energy error and fidelity almost monotonically for most frustration values. However, near $J_2/J_1=0.60$ ($N=10$) and over $J_2/J_1=0.60$--$1.00$ ($N=12$) the warm start stalls at a fidelity of $\approx 0.50$--$0.58$, although the energy error is small and the total spin stays in the $S=0$ sector. Removing the non-monotonic depth dependence is therefore not the same as reaching the ground state, and low energy and a singlet-like state are not sufficient: the fidelity, entropy and total spin must be satisfied together. The conclusions are limited to the system sizes and frustration values studied.

infographic.key_insight: Deeper symmetry-preserving VQE circuits can suffer an optimization collapse, while warm starts remove that collapse without guaranteeing the exact ground state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Identity-layer warm starts can stabilize depth scaling, but low energy and singlet character alone are insufficient indicators of ground-state accuracy.
method: Study 10- and 12-site frustrated J1–J2 Heisenberg rings using a Néel-initialized SingleExcitationMinus ansatz.
Compare random initialization with chained warm starts that append identity layers to optimized circuits.
Track fidelity, energy error, half-chain entropy and total spin across circuit depths.
infographic.evidence_signal: Random initialization shows abrupt degradation near depth 9 for 10 sites and depths 10–12 for 12 sites; warm starts remove the collapse but stall at approximately 0.50–0.58 fidelity in some frustration regimes.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to the studied sizes and frustration values; nested circuits and finite gradients support an optimization-failure explanation rather than lost expressibility or a barren plateau.
infographic.paper_title: Depth-Dependent Collapse and Warm-Start Limits of a Symmetry-Preserving VQE for the J$_1$--J$_2$ Heisenberg Ring
